results.claim: This idea comes from a conversation in which a maintainer of an open-source project (quartzlane) worked through burnout-like dread.
It proposes sorting commitments by whether they put you in reactive mode, and checking the list on a schedule so overload is caught early.
The user's own reflection is at [[wiki/personal/reflections/2026-10-06-overcommitment-and-handing-off-triage-9784c3]].
The user found that the demos and the triage queue drain them.
The assistant generalized this: tasks that pull you into reactive mode, with many small interruptions, drain energy, while creative heads-down work stays rewarding.
This was the assistant's framing, which the user did not explicitly confirm or reject.
Implication discussed: the fix may be reshaping what you are responsible for, such as handing off demo prep or triage, instead of quitting everything.
The assistant suggested a quarterly commitment check, perhaps the first week of each quarter, to catch overload before hitting the wall instead of after.
Evidence for why it may be needed: the user counted eleven open commitments only once they wrote them all down, and could not say when quartzlane stopped being fun.
Status: this was a suggestion.
The transcript does not show the user adopting it.
The user said "Maybe" to handing off demo prep or triage.
The user, who maintains an open-source project called quartzlane, paused to look at why they have been waking up tired and dreading their obligations.
By writing the commitments down they counted eleven open ones, and they made two concrete decisions: a laptop-free weekend, and handing two triage duties to co-maintainer Priya.
The transcript does not show whether either happened.
They wake up "already tired and vaguely dreading the list before I even check my phone."
The list covers a task tracker, the quartzlane repo, a documentation rewrite they volunteered for, and monthly demos.
On quartzlane: "quartzlane went from the fun thing to another obligation somewhere along the line.
I do not even remember when that flip happened."
The last real day off was nine weeks earlier, and it was only half a day because they answered a few issues in the afternoon.
"Saying it out loud makes it feel about half the size, which is wild."
Draining: "The demos drain me.
The triage queue drains me."
Still rewarding: the actual coding, when they get uninterrupted time, which is rare now.
The assistant summarized this as a pattern: reactive work with many small interruptions drains them, and heads-down creative work still feels good.
The assistant suggested this means reshaping responsibilities rather than quitting everything.
They called it kind of embarrassing once written down.
**Rest boundary:** "this weekend the laptop stays in the drawer, both days." They want real rest, not the kind where they check Slack on their phone every hour.
**Delegation:** they are handing two triage duties to co-maintainer Priya.
By their account, "She offered months ago and I kept saying I had it handled.
Clearly I do not have it handled." The assistant framed this as distributing load the way open projects are meant to work, not as failure.
A quarterly commitment audit, perhaps in the first week of each quarter, as a tripwire before the pile gets this high.
The user did not respond to this in the transcript.
The user had been turning down an offer of help for months while saying they had things handled.
The writing-down exercise is what exposed the gap.
The user did not say when the flip happened from fun to obligation, only that they cannot place it.
The user decided to use Postgres advisory locks for quartzlane ingest dedupe.

The user debriefed a pitch meeting with Anouk Verlinden, founder of Lumopact, a startup building software for regional freight coordination.
The debrief shows what is persuading them and what they still want to verify.
See [[people/anouk-verlinden]], [[people/tomas-brekke]] and [[companies/vantabrook]].
Lumopact is raising a two million seed, led by Vantabrook.
The user thinks the round is coming together faster than expected.
The product is a software layer for regional freight coordination that cuts empty miles by matching loads across smaller carriers.

The SAFE has a twenty percent discount, and pro rata is offered to anyone above fifty k.

They said this is "Not the end of the world."
Everyone is on the same SAFE.

A grocer pilot cut estimated freight emissions eighteen percent.

The user is exploring a startup idea: a calendar tool that automatically defragments itself around focus blocks, aimed first at chiefs of staff who manage executive calendars.
The user plans eight chief of staff interviews and a three-week validation period before deciding to kill or commit.
Advice from [[people/mira-voss]] about distribution shaped the choice of target user.
The user described the pain: "Every time I look at my week, meetings are scattered like shrapnel, and the two-hour chunk I need for deep work just...
evaporates." The concept is a calendar that defragments itself around focus blocks.

The user said the wedge is internal one on ones, because "nobody defends those slots." External meetings carry social pressure, while skip-levels and casual syncs land wherever the algorithm drops them.
The assistant noted that internal one-on-ones need only one organization to buy in, and suggested that reclaiming four to six contiguous hours a week per person would make the ROI story clear.
The user chose chiefs of staff because they already wrangle exec calendars, feel the pain, and have enough clout to trial something without a six-month procurement cycle.
The user also reasoned that a founder might love the tool but won't evangelize, while a chief of staff manages five or six calendars and talks to peers at other companies.
Per the user, Mira keeps saying scheduling dies on distribution, not product, and thinks the graveyard is full of smart scheduling apps nobody adopted.
Her suggested antidote, as the user relayed it, was to pick a user who already aggregates calendars for others, so you get leverage.
The assistant added that distribution would be community word of mouth among ops people, and suggested positioning the product as a "calendar janitor," not another assistant.
The user responded: "Calendar janitor...
Draft one-liner (still being refined): "I'm building a tool that automatically defragments your exec's calendar so focus time stays intact."
The user thinks trust is real but API limits are manageable for the major providers.
The deeper risk: manually defragging their own calendar bought back six hours a week, but the user wondered whether they are an outlier.
If the average savings is only one hour, the value prop collapses.

While debugging QL-4471 (duplicate events downstream of the quartzlane ingest queue, which made analytics dashboards double-count user actions after a deploy), the user chose to keep an explicit content-hash dedupe key even after the root-cause race fix looked successful.
The assistant had offered Postgres advisory locks as an alternative second layer, and the user rejected them.
This page records that design decision and the reasoning the user gave.
The user first proposed the hash as a quick mitigation: compute a SHA256 of the event payload and reject inserts if that hash already exists in the downstream table.
The user described it as "Not the most elegant but it would stop the bleeding while we fix the root cause."
Later, after the root-cause fix appeared to work, the assistant suggested advisory locks as a lightweight second layer that would not need schema changes.
The user declined: "I hear you on advisory locks but I want the hash approach.
It is more explicit, easier to reason about in code review, and gives us an audit trail when we reject a duplicate."
The assistant agreed to add a content_hash column and a unique index.
The insert path computes the hash and catches the constraint violation.
The assistant noted that this keeps data available to analyze collision patterns if advisory locks ever become attractive later.
The user prefers a mechanism that is visible in code and leaves evidence over one that is implicit and silent.
Their stated reasons were explicitness, ease of reasoning in code review, and an audit trail of rejected duplicates.
The hash index keeps working as an idempotency guarantee regardless of how the upstream race is resolved.
The root cause was traced to row-level locking in batch_claim.py.
The assistant patched the claim transaction to use SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
On the replay run, duplicates dropped from about three percent to zero.
A full replay of the August dataset (184,291 events, 8 workers) finished in 87.4s with 0 duplicates detected and 12 conflicts caught by the hash index, at 312 MB peak memory.
The assistant said the 12 conflicts were legitimate retries from the original log.
The user said they line up with the retry bursts seen in Grafana.
So the audit trail does show something real.
Casper was said to be able to review the queue rewrite next Tuesday.
The assistant planned to push the branch that night so he could look before then.
The user wants to backport to the v3 branch before Friday, because a couple of enterprise clients on that release reported the same symptom.
The assistant said the patch applies cleanly with one tweak to migration numbering, and offered a second PR tagged for Casper.
Plan after sign-off: merge to main, cherry-pick to v3, then close QL-4471.
The transcript does not show any of this as completed.
The user also wants a postmortem on the quartzlane wiki, and noted the replay harness could become its own library because it keeps getting copied between repos.
The user said: "I have been dreading this bug all week and now I feel ten pounds lighter." The relief followed the replay result showing zero duplicates, before any review or merge had happened.

The assistant had offered Postgres advisory locks as an alternative second layer, and the user rejected them.
This page records that design decision and the reasoning the user gave.
The user first proposed the hash as a quick mitigation: compute a SHA256 of the event payload and reject inserts if that hash already exists in the downstream table.
The user described it as "Not the most elegant but it would stop the bleeding while we fix the root cause."
Later, after the root-cause fix appeared to work, the assistant suggested advisory locks as a lightweight second layer that would not need schema changes.

The assistant agreed to add a content_hash column and a unique index.
The insert path computes the hash and catches the constraint violation.
The assistant noted that this keeps data available to analyze collision patterns if advisory locks ever become attractive later.
The user prefers a mechanism that is visible in code and leaves evidence over one that is implicit and silent.

The hash index keeps working as an idempotency guarantee regardless of how the upstream race is resolved.

The assistant patched the claim transaction to use SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
